clue.text: Bill takes cover under trees to see bird

indicators.note: in a down clue, sheltering beneath something means being written below it in the column

parts.note: a greenwood is a forest in leaf
a pecker is a bird's beak, so a bill

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher hides under the trees to spot something on the wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name; it is a beak, and its word is written below the trees because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The green woodpecker is a common European species of woodpecker with green plumage.

clue.text: Fair, fashionable, good popular newspaper!

parts.note: fair as in balanced or level
what is in is in fashion
G is the usual abbreviation for good
standard in the sense of usual or widely adopted

explanation.surface: A string of compliments for a well-liked newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Evening Standard is London's evening newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The Evening Standard is a daily London paper, a specific example of a newspaper.

clue.text: Used to write and rewrite notes at table

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a writing machine rather than a noun

indicators.note: to rewrite something is to set it down again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a graph and a table both present data

explanation.surface: Someone sits at a table writing and rewriting notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' here means placed next to: the rearranged notes sit beside the table.
explanation.definitionFit: A stenograph is a shorthand typing machine, the device a court reporter uses to write.

clue.text: Foolish, crazy, insane and initially incomprehensible

indicators.note: something crazy is disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: the first letter of incomprehensible

explanation.surface: A list of insults for a baffling, mad idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' and 'insane' both look like synonyms of the definition; one is the signal and the other is the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine means stupid, literally donkey-like, a close synonym of foolish.

clue.text: Elizabeth's about to help

indicators.note: the name is wrapped around the word wanted, so it sits inside the name's letters

parts.note: found inside the name, after its first four letters

explanation.surface: Elizabeth is just about to lend a hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to assist or encourage, usually in wrongdoing, so a synonym of help.

clue.text: Fern and Tom hoping to get spread in "Hello!"

indicators.note: letters spread out are scattered and can be laid down in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two celebrities, Fern and Tom, hope for a photo spread in Hello! magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a British celebrity magazine, which is why the surface talks of a spread; here the word is just a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Top of the morning is a traditional, stereotypically Irish greeting, an old-fashioned way of saying good morning.

clue.text: Research and observe certain matter at university

parts.note: to look is to observe
an unspecified thing
a British student is up at university

explanation.surface: A student studies and watches something at university.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a student is 'up' while at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge, and 'goes down' when leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: To look something up is to search for information in a reference, a form of research.

clue.text: Tommy's naughty bits

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ordinary British soldiers, nicknamed Tommies
second meaning: the genitals, in a coy euphemism

explanation.walkthrough: Tommy is the old nickname for a British private soldier; the surface reads it as one man's possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Privates are the lowest-ranked soldiers and also a polite euphemism for the genitals.

clue.text: Twice expressing contempt for mistake

wordplay.note: the jeer a crowd shouts in scorn, said two times over

explanation.surface: Someone jeers twice at a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A boo-boo is an informal, childish word for a silly error or blunder.

clue.text: Chap's against Enron restructuring

parts.note: V for versus

indicators.note: restructuring a company reorganises it, so these letters are reorganised too

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A man opposes reorganising the collapsed energy firm Enron.
explanation.walkthrough: Enron was an American energy company that collapsed in a 2001 fraud scandal; the 's is short for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vernon is a man's first name, and in crosswords 'chap' can clue any male name.

clue.text: Meshes and knots were almost undone

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
knots that are undone come apart, and the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Knotted nets were nearly untied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meshes and knots' looks like a list; 'and' is the join between definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A mesh is a net of interlaced strands, and networks are such interlinked webs.

clue.text: Perhaps Keats regularly saw Fanny?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Keats often met his sweetheart Fanny Brawne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' looks as if it goes with Keats; it governs the two words after it. Fanny Brawne was Keats's beloved.
explanation.definitionFit: A great poet is poetically called a swan, as Shakespeare is the Swan of Avon, and Keats is one example.

clue.text: Creating a limited amount of DNA

parts.note: a gene is a stretch of DNA
a ration is a fixed, limited allowance

explanation.surface: Making only a small quantity of genetic material.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in reverse order to the clue: the ration is of gene, so gene comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Generation is the act of producing or bringing something into being, a noun matching creating used as a noun.

clue.text: Wild harebell is delightful

indicators.note: wild means unruly or untamed, so the letters run riot

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A harebell growing wild is a lovely sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild harebell' reads as a single flower; 'Wild' is the signal. A harebell is a blue bellflower.
explanation.definitionFit: Something relishable can be enjoyed with relish, so it gives pleasure, a near synonym of delightful.

clue.text: Reformatory — first element of betterment or last resort?

indicators.note: the first element of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter

indicators.note: read as re-sort, meaning sort again, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then re-sorted

explanation.surface: Is a reform school a first step toward improvement or a place of last resort?
explanation.walkthrough: 'last resort' looks like a set phrase; split resort as re-sort. A borstal was a British detention centre for young offenders.
explanation.definitionFit: A reformatory is an institution for reforming young offenders, which is what the British borstal was.

clue.text: Kipper tie for an American

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one who kips, that is, sleeps
second meaning: the British word for the timber beneath rails that Americans call a tie

explanation.walkthrough: A kipper tie is a very wide 1960s necktie, which is the false trail; to kip is British slang for to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: One who sleeps is a sleeper, and in Britain a sleeper is also a railway tie.

clue.text: EU policy ultimately provides support for angry, headstrong people

indicators.note: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so the following pieces go below the next one

parts.note: mad meaning furious
the Common Agricultural Policy of the European Union

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: European farming policy props up furious, stubborn people.
explanation.walkthrough: The CAP is the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, often blamed for subsidising farmers.
explanation.definitionFit: A madcap is a reckless, impulsive person, close to headstrong in sense.

clue.text: Campaign leaders passed her a cocktail

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mix, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Political organisers hand a woman a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Spearheads are those at the front of an effort, the people or groups leading a campaign.

clue.text: Cleaner finally got rid of brownish mark

indicators.note: getting rid of something removes it, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: ochre is a yellowish-brown earth colour

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A cleaner at last removed a brown stain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleaner' and 'got rid of brownish mark' make a cleaning scene, but mark is the definition: the oche is the line darts players stand behind.
explanation.definitionFit: The oche is the line marked on the floor behind which a darts player must stand to throw.

clue.text: Learned America's about to have a Democrat in charge

parts.note: A is a standard abbreviation for America
C for circa, Latin for about
taken as written
the short form of Democrat
IC is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: The US is set to be run by a Democratic leader, which some would call a learned choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Academic means scholarly, so it matches learned used as an adjective pronounced in two syllables.

clue.text: Philosopher married badly

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married
ill as an adverb, as in ill-treated

explanation.surface: A thinker who made an unhappy marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: John Stuart Mill was a nineteenth-century English philosopher, author of On Liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: John Stuart Mill, the utilitarian thinker, is a famous example of a philosopher.

clue.text: It keeps sun off part of lawn in Granada

indicators.note: part of says the word wanted is a stretch of the letters that follow

parts.note: runs across the three words, starting after the first letter

explanation.surface: Something shades part of a lawn in the Spanish city of Granada.
explanation.definitionFit: An awning is a canvas sheet stretched over a window or terrace to give shade.

clue.text: Lauren's volatile and nervy

definitions.note: read as relating to the nerves

indicators.note: something volatile is unstable and changes readily, so the letters will not keep their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Lauren is temperamental and anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nervy' usually means jittery; here it is taken literally as having to do with nerves.
explanation.definitionFit: Neural means of the nerves or nervous system, a sense nervy can bear in a literal reading.

clue.text: He famously advised murder weapon to be changed at last

indicators.note: changed at last says only the end of the word is altered, its final letter swapped

parts.note: the radioactive element used to poison Alexander Litvinenko in London in 2006

explanation.surface: A detective suggests the murder weapon should be swapped at the last moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The final M is swapped for S. Polonius in Hamlet gives his son Laertes famous advice, including 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be'.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius is the Shakespearean courtier best known for his string of advice to his departing son.
